newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan exchange pushes on with coffee futures plan.
newsitem.headline: Japan exchange pushes on with coffee futures plan.

text.p: The Tokyo Grain Exchange (TGE) is forging ahead with a long-standing plan to launch a coffee futures contract in Japan, the world's third largest consumer of the bean.
But the exchange is facing strong opposition from local coffee roasters, who are mainly concerned that the transparency of coffee prices will deprive them of their price-setting role.
The TGE set up a committee in March to study the listing of a coffee futures contract and aims to finalise the details by this September, TGE officials say.
"We believe it's more convenient to have a coffee futures contract here as Japan's coffee consumption is pretty large," said Keiji Hatano, the manager of the TGE's planning department.

"The new contract will provide a risk hedging tool as volatility of coffee futures is high. But we can't say when we will be able to launch the contract, since we can't go ahead with the plan without obtaining the industry's consent," he told Reuters in an interview.
The idea of launching a coffee futures contract first sprang up in 1987, but plans have been on hold due mainly to opposition from the local coffee industry.

But with Japan's emergence as a major consumer of commodities, the government has decided to promote the commodities futures trade and one way of doing that is by providing the means to hedge price risks.
Japan is the world's third largest consumer of coffee after the United States and Germany. Japan's green coffee imports in calendar 1996 totalled 326,388 tonnes, Finance Ministry data showed.
Industry sources said a coffee futures market would not be successful without the local industry's support.

"The project will be doomed if the industry continues to stick to its opposition, as a coffee futures contract is a rather difficult product to launch," said Masao Yamashita, executive director of the All Japan Coffee Association.

The TGE's Hatano also echoed that view, saying that an acceptable selection of coffee beans will be hard without the industry's cooperation since there are a wide variety of beans and different tastes.
"The quality standard for coffee in Japan is rather high. We see there will be no reason to launch the contract if we list a product that is unacceptable to the industry," he said.
Coffee industry sources say most of the estimated 400 roasters in Japan do not see much of a need for a coffee futures contract in Tokyo.
"One main reason behind the opposition is that coffee roasters are afraid coffee prices will be transparent when the yen-based coffee prices are launched," a manager at a commodities broker said.

"They are currently setting prices based on New York's Coffee and Cocoa Exchange, and there may be some vague Japanese premiums. But once yen-based prices are established, the transparency in prices could deprive roasters of some of the benefits they now enjoy," the manager said.

Commodity brokers say, however, that Japan's need to expand the listing of commodity futures contracts will be essential in the future as current regulations restricting commodity futures trading may be eased ahead of the Japanese government's "Big Bang" financial reforms.
